x: At the end of the Common, Harry Churcher was well away in the lead followed by D. McMullen, Copperwheat, Miller and Tunbridge and it was evident that Churcher was going to cut out a very fast pace.

This race produced the largest field so far of the season and of the 205 starters, Harry Churcher soon went to the front and walked a very fast race to finish well ahead of Jim Morris who was making one of his rare appearances.
At the start of the race Sheffield received a serious blow in the disqualification of Proctor who joined in an extremely fast start with his team mates Allen and Hardy and our own Harry Churcher.
All our lads started fairly steady and at three miles Charlie Churcher and Bob McMullen were in 5th and 6th positions, whilst Bob Readman and George Oliver were together at 15th.

Charlie Churcher was taking a bashing but quite enjoying it and there were hopes he might catch Goodall, Woodford's 2nd man. Pat Sapcote was determinedly chasing three Woodford men and the odds seemed that he would catch them, in fact he assured us that it was in the bag, and he certainly did it.
At this point, George Coleman had a few yards' advantage over the Belgrave trio, Gregory, Churcher and McMullen—well stimulated by the exhortations of numerous "Bels" supporters.
A small exercise book titled “Walking Records 1929” was compiled by Harry Churcher one of our greatest short distance men in the ’thirties and ’forties.
